title: Work and Vocation: A Bible Study on Faith and Your Job
subtitle: A five-session study on work and vocation, and the faith that has to survive Monday.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes and anyone who has sat in church on Sunday feeling that their faith was real and large, then walked into work on Monday and watched it shrink to nothing. It's for the believer who suspects, somewhere underneath, that God's real work happens on a stage with a microphone and that their own forty hours at a desk or a register or a job site are spiritually beside the point. Over five sessions it asks what work is and was meant to be: Eden, where God himself worked and called it good; the thorns and sweat that came after; the lie that splits the world into sacred jobs and secular ones; the idol work becomes when it stops being what we do and starts being who we are; and the strange promise that our labor isn't finally lost. It's built so a busy volunteer can lead it. Every question comes with notes on what's behind it, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This study won't tell you to find your passion and let the rest take care of itself, because most work isn't passion and most weeks aren't inspiring, and the gospel has something to say to an ordinary Tuesday, not only to the calling that thrills you. It refuses two lies at once. The first says ordinary work doesn't matter to God, that only ministry counts, and the study takes that apart with Luther, Dorothy Sayers and the doctrine of vocation. The second says work is everything, the place we earn our worth and prove we exist, and the study names that as the idol it is. And it starts with the pastor. The pastorate is a job too, one that can be loved into an idol and hidden behind, its busyness called faithfulness when it's really fear. The teaching speaks from inside that problem, and it asks you to do the same.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Before the Thorns
sessions.aim: To recover what the church keeps forgetting: work is older than sin. It was given in the garden before anything broke, as part of the good creation and the image of a God who himself works, and it isn't the punishment we secretly think it is.
sessions.summary:
After a long week people often joke that they can't wait for heaven, because they'll never have to work again. It's said as a joke, and it isn't one. Underneath it sits a belief most Christians hold without examining it: work is a curse, imposed when Adam sinned, and we'll be rid of it when we're saved.

The first question of this study is whether that's true, and it isn't. Open Genesis and the first worker in the Bible is God. He works for six days and calls the work good. Then he makes a creature in his image, and the first thing he gives that creature is a job: "The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). That's before the serpent, before the fruit, before the thorns.

Something did go wrong with work, and Genesis 3 says so plainly. But the curse fell on work that already existed. It didn't invent work. To be made in the image of a working God is to be made to work, to make and cultivate and bring order out of raw material the way he did. So the believer who despises all work as a necessary evil isn't being spiritual. He's mourning a curse where God gave a gift.

keyScripture.why: "The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). God put a job in human hands before anything had gone wrong, so work belongs to the good creation and not to the fall.

discussion.q: Before tonight, did you think of work as a blessing, a curse, or a necessary evil you put up with to pay for the parts of life that really matter?
discussion.behind: Bring the default into the open before correcting anything. Most people carry an unexamined verdict on their own work, and it's usually a low one: something endured rather than received. You're not settling it yet. Let people say what they actually think. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 1:31-2:3. The first worker in the Bible is God, working for six days and calling the work good. What does it do to your view of your own job to start there, with work as something God does rather than a human punishment?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the curse reflex. We assume work began when things went wrong. Help people notice that God worked before any creature did and called the work good, so labor has dignity at the root. Let them feel what it means to be made in the image of a God who makes.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 2:15-20. God gave Adam a job before the fall. Why do you think the church so often talks as if work itself were the problem, rather than what the fall did to work?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. Keep it on the assumptions people live by, not abstract theology. We mourn a curse where God gave a gift. Help the room see that despising all work as a necessary evil isn't a spiritual posture. It's a failure to read past chapter three.

discussion.q: Being made in the image of a working God means being made to make, to cultivate, to bring order out of raw material. Where in your own work, however ordinary, have you felt a flicker of being made for this?
discussion.behind: Move from doctrine to recognition. You aren't looking for people with glamorous jobs. The accountant bringing order to a mess, the parent making a home out of ordinary days, the welder joining what was apart: all of it bears the image. Help even the weary find the dignity in their week. Go first.

discussion.q: Many of us treat work as the thing standing between us and the life we really want. Where have you done that, living for the weekend or for retirement, as if the work itself were the enemy?
discussion.behind: Bring everyone inside. You aren't adding guilt; you're naming a quiet despair many of us carry, that most of our waking hours are something to be survived. The gospel reaches our Mondays only after we admit how little we expected God to be there. Go first.

objections.objection: Work is obviously a curse. Genesis says it plainly: cursed is the ground because of you, and by the sweat of your face you'll eat. The Bible itself calls work a consequence of sin, so don't dress it up as a gift.
objections.response: Part of this is true. Something did go wrong with work, and Genesis names it without flinching: thorns, sweat and futility, all real and all the result of the fall. We'll spend the whole next session inside that curse, because this study won't pretend Monday doesn't hurt. But look carefully at where the curse falls. It falls on work that was already there. Adam was working the garden in chapter 2, before the serpent said a word, given the job by God himself as part of bearing his image. The curse didn't create work. It corrupted work the Creator had already given and called good. To call work a curse is to confuse the wound with the body that was wounded. Work is Eden's gift. The thorns are what the fall did to it, and that difference is the whole point.

objections.objection: If work is so good and so much part of God's design, why does the Bible end with rest, with no more curse and no more toil? Heaven is the end of work, which proves work was never the point.
objections.response: There's real truth here. Scripture does end in rest, and the toil and futility, the cursed parts of work, are gone for good. That's a mercy worth longing for. But look closely at what the end of the Bible pictures, because it isn't an eternity of idleness. "His servants will worship him" (Revelation 22:3), and the kings of the earth "bring their glory into" the city (Revelation 21:24). What ends isn't work but the curse on work: the sweat, the thorns, the sense that it's all for nothing. God's rest isn't the absence of all activity. It's the end of striving and futility, work freed at last to be what Eden meant it to be. Heaven isn't the abolition of work. It's its redemption, and we'll get there in session 5.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the work you spend most of your waking hours doing, and when did you last let yourself believe God was in it and pleased with it, rather than waiting for you somewhere else?
sessions.practice: This week, pick one ordinary task in your work, the most routine thing you do. Before you begin it, say out loud that this is part of how you bear the image of a God who works. Then do it with attention, as if it mattered, because it does. At the end of the week, write down whether naming the dignity of the task changed how it felt to do it, even a little, even once.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you worked before any of us did, and you called the working good. Then you made us in your image and put work into our hands as a gift before anything had broken. Forgive us for despising what you blessed, and for treating most of our lives as a sentence to be served. Teach us to see our labor the way you saw your own over those six days: as good, as ours, as one of the ways we're like you. Meet us in the ordinary work of our hands, and let us find you there. Amen.
reflection: Where have I called work a curse when God called it good, and what would change if I read my own week as part of the image I bear rather than a punishment I serve?
When I imagine the life I really want, is there any work in it, and what does that tell me about what I think work is for?
If God gave Adam a job before the fall, what does that say about whether my ordinary work matters to God today, before I get anywhere better?
sessions.teaching:
Start with a familiar line, the one people say after a long week, half laughing: they can't wait for heaven, because then they'll never have to work again. Everyone laughs. But under the joke sits a conviction almost every Christian carries without examining it. Work is a curse. It's what God hung on us when Adam sinned, the price of the fall, the burden we'll finally lay down when we're saved. Heaven, in this picture, is the great vacation, the end of the alarm clock. And if that's true, then the forty or fifty or sixty hours most of us spend at work each week are a kind of waiting room, something to endure until real life begins.

So before we go anywhere else, we have to ask whether it's true. It isn't.

Open the Bible to its first page and notice who the first worker is. It isn't Adam. It's God. "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1), and the language of Genesis 1 is the language of a craftsman at a bench: separating, forming, filling, ordering. Six days of work, and at the end he steps back and looks: "And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). Even his rest is described in terms of work: "on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested" (Genesis 2:2). The first thing the Bible tells you about God is that he works, and that his work is good.

That matters more than we let it. God then makes a creature in his own image, and the first thing he does with that creature, before the fall, before a single thing has gone wrong, is give him a job. "The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). Adam is a gardener before he's anything else. God brings him the animals "to see what he would call them" (Genesis 2:19), which is the work of a scientist and a poet at once. He's given a world of raw material and told to cultivate it, to bring order and beauty and fruit out of it, the way his Maker brought a world out of the formless deep. Work is in Eden. It's part of the original good, woven into what it means to be human and to bear the image of a God who works.

Now take the objection at full strength, because it's a fair one and the text is right there. Doesn't Genesis say, "cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life" (Genesis 3:17)? It does, and we'll spend the whole next session inside those words, because this study has no interest in pretending Monday doesn't hurt. Something did go wrong with work. The thorns are real. But look at where the curse lands. It lands on work that already existed. The sweat and the futility didn't invent work. They corrupted a work God had already given and already called good, a chapter earlier. The fall didn't create labor; it vandalized it.

So to call work itself a curse is to make a basic mistake, like confusing the graffiti with the wall. Work is the wall. Sin is the graffiti. They aren't the same thing, and the whole question of how a Christian should think about Monday turns on telling them apart. Work isn't the curse. It's the gift the curse fell on. A believer who despises all labor as a necessary evil to be escaped isn't more spiritual than the rest of us. He's less biblical. He's mourning a gift and calling the mourning faith.

We have to stand inside this, because most of us have done it for years. We treat our own work, even the work of ministry, as the thing standing between us and the life we wanted. We live for the day off and the vacation and the eventual rest, as though God were waiting for us on the far side of our labor instead of present in the middle of it. The joke about never working again just says out loud what many of us believe in silence.

So we begin by going back before the thorns, to the garden where God worked, called it good, put a job in human hands, and pronounced the whole arrangement, the worker and the work together, very good. That's where your Monday actually comes from. Not from the fall. From the goodness of God.

scriptureStudy.note: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth." The first thing Scripture says about God is that he makes. Before any human works, God is already at work, so work is godlike before it's ever a burden.

"And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." The Creator looks over his finished work and pronounces it good, the way a craftsman steps back from the bench. Work has dignity at the root because God himself worked.

"On the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work." Even God's rest is rest from finished work, not idleness. The rhythm of work and rest is built into creation before sin enters.

"The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it." The first assignment given to the first human is a job, in Eden, before the fall. Work is the original calling, not the consequence of sin.

"The LORD God... brought them to the man to see what he would call them." Naming is the work of ordering and understanding the world, creative and intellectual labor handed to the image-bearer before anything breaks.
"Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion." The first blessing on humanity is a charge to cultivate and care for creation, given as a blessing and not a burden.

"You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet." The psalmist sees human work as a share in God's own rule over creation, which makes the worker a steward, not a slave.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at the long argument the church has had with itself about whether work is noble or base, because the idea that labor is beneath the truly spiritual life is older than any of us and has done real damage. In much of the ancient world, manual work belonged to slaves and the lower orders, and the contemplative life of the mind was counted higher. The church partly absorbed that ranking, so that for long stretches the monk at prayer was thought to be doing holier work than the farmer in the field. There was a real insight in it: not all of life reduces to production, and the soul has a calling beyond the paycheck. But it hardened into a lie, a sacred tier of work that counts to God and a secular tier that doesn't, and session 3 takes that lie apart.

Set that against Genesis, where God works, the first human is a laborer, and the dignity of work is established before any priest or temple exists. Weigh both the wisdom and the error in the older view. Honor the truth that we're more than what we produce, and reject the falsehood that ordinary labor is spiritually second-class. Lester DeKoster, in his short book Work: The Meaning of Your Life (1982), argues that work is how we make ourselves useful to others, and so one of the main ways we love our neighbor. Hold that up against any theology that treats the daily grind as beneath God's notice.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman raising three children at home has stopped saying what she does when people ask, because "just a mom" always comes out like an apology. She has sat through years of sermons celebrating people who left their careers for the mission field and felt, every time, that her own days of laundry, meals and the slow shaping of small souls were the part of life God was waiting out.

Walk the group through her week with the eyes of Genesis. She's bringing order out of chaos, cultivating, making a home out of ordinary days. She's working as an image-bearer in the most literal sense. Ask the group where they, like her, have apologized for ordinary work that God himself gave dignity to. The point isn't to flatter her. It's to help everyone see that the gift of work in the garden reaches all the way down into the unglamorous and unpaid labor most of us actually do.

sessions.title: Thorns and Sweat
sessions.aim: To tell the truth about why Monday feels the way it does: to name the curse on work without explaining it away, and to refuse both the lie that good work always feels satisfying and the despair that says it's all for nothing.
sessions.summary:
If work was a gift, why does so much of it feel like punishment? This session won't dodge that. The same Genesis that puts a job in human hands before the fall says after it, "cursed is the ground because of you... thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you... By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread" (Genesis 3:17-19). The curse isn't spoken over the worker. It's spoken over the ground, so the same task now resists the hand that does it. Work that flowed becomes work that fights back.

The cynic says this is simply how things are: work is meaningless toil, and Ecclesiastes is right that it's all "vanity and a striving after wind" (Ecclesiastes 2:11). Scripture itself grants the weight of that. The Preacher really does say, "I hated all my toil" (Ecclesiastes 2:18). The futility is in the Bible. But the curse isn't the first word about work, and it isn't the last. It's the long, hard middle of the story most of us live in, between the garden where work was good and the new creation where it will be good again.

Naming the thorns plainly is a mercy. A believer who's been told that good Christian work should always feel meaningful is being set up to despair on the first grinding, thankless Tuesday. The curse explains the grind. A faith that can't account for the grind won't survive Monday.

keyScripture.why: "Cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you... By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread" (Genesis 3:17-19). The curse falls on the ground, so labor now resists the laborer. These verses give plain words for why Monday feels the way it does.

discussion.q: If work was a gift in the garden, why do you think so much of your own work feels like a grind, something you push through rather than something you enjoy?
discussion.behind: Start with experience before doctrine. Let people say how heavy work can feel, and don't rush to fix it. You're bringing out the gap between the good gift of session 1 and the actual Monday, because that gap is exactly what the curse explains.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 3:17-19. The curse falls on the ground, not on the worker; thorns come up to resist the hand that works. How does it land to hear that the resistance you feel in your work may be the world being broken, not you failing?
discussion.behind: Many people read their frustration at work as personal inadequacy. Help them move the problem from the worker to the cursed ground, which is both truer and freeing, without letting anyone use it as an excuse to stop trying.

discussion.q: Read Ecclesiastes 2:17-23. The Preacher calls his work vanity and says he hated his toil. What's true in that, and what does it miss about where the curse sits in the whole story?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Ecclesiastes really does name the futility, and no one should leave thinking the Bible is naive about meaningless toil. The miss is treating the curse as the first and last word when it's the middle. Help people place the grind between Eden and the new creation.

discussion.q: Where have you believed that if your work were the right work, it would always feel meaningful? What has that belief done to you on the ordinary, thankless days?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. The culture sells a gospel of passion and fulfilling work, and it sets believers up to despair when most weeks aren't inspiring. Press gently on the lie that good work should always feel good, and on how it makes the normal grind feel like proof something is wrong.

discussion.q: Most of us have mornings when we resent even the work we believe we were called to. Where have you resented your own work, and what would it mean to say so without shame?
discussion.behind: Close by bringing everyone inside. The point is permission, not confession-hunting. Even good and called work can feel like sweat and thorns, and saying so is healthier than pretending. Go first, and keep it gentle. Let people stop performing a satisfaction they don't feel.

objections.objection: Work is just meaningless toil. Ecclesiastes is right: it's all vanity. You labor your whole life and then leave it to someone who didn't earn it and will waste it. There's no dignity in the grind, only the grind.
objections.response: Don't win this cheaply, because Scripture itself grants its weight. The Preacher says, "I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool?" (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19). The futility is in the Bible, named without flinching, and any faith worth having has to reckon with it. But notice where the futility sits in the larger story. It isn't the first word about work, which was good, and it isn't the last, which is the new creation. It's the long middle. Ecclesiastes tells the truth about work "under the sun," work cut off from God and treated as the only thing there is. It doesn't tell the whole truth about work under the eye of a Creator who gave it and a Redeemer who won't let it be lost. The vanity is real, but it isn't final.

objections.objection: So the answer is that work is supposed to be miserable and I should just accept it as my lot. If the curse explains the grind, I should expect nothing better and stop hoping work could be good.
objections.response: No. The curse is an explanation, not a sentence to passivity. Naming that the ground is cursed doesn't mean we bless the thorns and stop pulling them. Much of the calling of work after the fall is to push back against the curse: to bring order where there's chaos and make things grow where the ground resists, which is a small share in the redemption God is working. The curse explains why work fights back. It doesn't tell you to surrender. Nor does it mean work is now only misery, because grace breaks into the middle of the story, and there are real goods and real satisfactions, moments when the gift of Eden shows through even now. The curse accounts for the grind so you don't despair when it comes. It doesn't ask you to stop hoping, or stop working, for the good work was meant to be.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What part of your work feels most like pulling thorns, the resistance you push against week after week, and have you ever told anyone how heavy it is?
sessions.practice: This week, when the resistance comes, the thankless task, the thing that fights back, don't call it your failure and don't pretend it doesn't weigh on you. Name it for what it is, out loud or on paper: the ground resisting the hand, the curse and not your inadequacy. Then get to work anyway, as someone pushing back against the thorns. Write down whether naming it plainly changed how you carried it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you gave us work as a gift, and then the world broke, and now the ground itself resists the hand that works it, and we've carried that resistance as though it were our own failure. We're tired. Some of us dread the morning. Forgive us for the lie that good work should always feel good, and for the despair that says it's all for nothing. You haven't abandoned us to the thorns. Your Son wore them on his head, and you're redeeming even our hardest labor. Meet us in the sweat of our weeks, and give us strength to keep pulling thorns until the curse is lifted for good. Amen.
reflection: Where have I read the resistance in my work as proof that I'm failing, when it may be the broken world fighting back?
Have I been waiting for work that finally feels meaningful all the time, and what has that done to me on the ordinary, grinding days?
What does it mean that the curse is the middle of the story and not the end, and how would Monday feel if I believed the thorns were temporary?
sessions.teaching:
We ended last week in the garden, with work as a gift: a God who worked and called it good, and put a job in human hands before anything broke. If we stopped there, this study would be a lie, because none of us lives in Genesis 2. We live in chapter 3 and everything after it, and chapter 3 is where the thorns come in. So this week we have to be more truthful than the church often is about why work that was a gift so often feels like punishment.

Genesis doesn't dodge the question, and neither will we. After the man and the woman eat, God speaks the consequences, and notice where the curse on work falls. "Cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you... By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread" (Genesis 3:17-19). Not "cursed are you," but "cursed is the ground." The curse doesn't land on the worker. It lands on the material the worker works with. The same labor that flowed in the garden now fights back. Thorns come up where you planted wheat. The harvest fails for reasons you can't control. The project collapses after months of effort. The customer is cruel, the boss is unreasonable, the body breaks down, the spreadsheet won't balance, and the children you're raising push against every good thing you try to plant in them. By the next chapter, God is telling Cain, "When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength" (Genesis 4:12). Work isn't abolished; it's frustrated.

There's something freeing buried in that. The resistance you feel in your work isn't first of all evidence that you're bad at it. It's evidence that the world is broken. The thorns aren't your inadequacy; they're the curse.

Now take the cynic at full strength, because his voice is in the Bible itself, and a faith that can't face him is too thin to bother with. The Preacher of Ecclesiastes looks at everything he's built and says, "behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 2:11). "I hated all my toil," he says, because he has to leave it to whoever comes after him, "and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool?" (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19). That's in your Bible, flatly, without comfort, and we mustn't wave it off with a verse. There are days and seasons and whole careers when work feels exactly like this: building what will be torn down, pouring yourself into what no one will remember. Grant it: the vanity is real.

But ask where the futility sits in the whole story, because the cynic makes one mistake. He treats the curse as the first word and the last, when it's the middle. The first word about work was good, the gift of Eden. The last word, as we'll see, is redemption. Paul names the same futility Ecclesiastes felt, "the creation was subjected to futility," and then says it was subjected "in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption" (Romans 8:20-21). Ecclesiastes tells the truth about work under the sun, cut off from God. It isn't the whole truth about work under the eye of the God who gave it and the Christ who is redeeming it.

That's why naming the thorns isn't pessimism. It's mercy. Think of the believer who has never been told this. He has absorbed, from the culture and sometimes from the church, a gospel of fulfilling work: find the right job, your true calling, your passion, and work will be deeply satisfying, and the satisfaction will prove you're where God wants you. Then he gets the job, and most of it is ordinary, some of it is tedious, and a great deal of it is thankless, and the first joyless Tuesday hits him like a verdict. Something must be wrong. Wrong job. Wrong calling. Wrong with me. He's set up to despair, or to quit, or to keep chasing work that will finally feel the way the lie promised, which doesn't exist. The doctrine of the curse rescues him. The grind isn't a sign he's in the wrong place. It's the condition of all work this side of Eden, and the right job will have thorns too. A faith that can't account for the grind won't survive Monday.

No one lives outside the thorns, pastors included. Most of us have resented even the work we were surest God called us to. There are mornings when called work feels like pulling weeds, weeks when a preacher stands up with no fire in him. Pastors tend to hide that, because they're supposed to be above it, and that's its own kind of lie. So let it be said plainly, so you can say it too. The thorns are real, even in good work. Your dread on a Monday isn't proof your faith has failed. It's proof you're working cursed ground, like every other child of Adam.

But we don't pull thorns forever. "The soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head" (John 19:2). Christ wore the curse, and the day is coming when the ground will be free. Until then we work the broken field without the lie that it should feel like Eden and without the despair that says it's only vanity. The curse is the middle of the story. We don't live at the end yet, but we know how it ends.

scriptureStudy.note: "Cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life." The curse falls on the ground, the material of work, not on the worker, so labor now resists the laborer. The frustration of work is the world broken, not the soul failing.

"Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you... By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread." Work now comes mixed with sweat and resistance: the gift corrupted but not destroyed. This is why even good work fights back.

"Behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun." The Preacher names the futility of work under the sun without comfort, and Scripture lets the complaint stand.

"I hated all my toil... seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool?" The fear that our work will be wasted by whoever inherits it is named plainly here: the curse felt as the fear that nothing lasts.

"For the creation was subjected to futility... in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption." Paul names the same futility Ecclesiastes felt but places it in a story with an ending: a creation groaning toward freedom.

"When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength." Spoken to Cain, it shows the curse on work deepening with sin, the ground withholding its strength and the worker estranged from the fruit of his labor.

"And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head." The sign of the curse on work, the thorn, is pressed onto the head of Christ, the first hint that the thorns won't have the last word.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at the tradition of lament about work that runs through Scripture and the church, because a faith that only celebrates work and never grieves its frustration isn't the faith of the Bible. Ecclesiastes is the great example. The church has often been embarrassed by it, because it refuses easy comfort and stares at the vanity of toil without blinking, yet it sits in the canon because God's people need permission to say that work sometimes feels meaningless.

Set this beside our own time, when the culture has swung to the opposite error, preaching that work should be your passion, your identity and the source of your meaning. That gospel of fulfilling work crushes the ordinary worker the moment the job turns dull or hard. Weigh both errors, the cynicism that says work is only vanity and the romanticism that says work should always thrill, and ask which has shaped you more. Tim Keller, in Every Good Endeavor (2012), writes about both the dignity of work in its design and its frustration since the fall, and argues that a Christian holds both rather than collapsing into the cynic's despair or the romantic's disappointment. The discipline here is to recover the lost practice of lament over work: to say that the grind is real and heavy while refusing the lie that the grind is the whole truth.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group spent eleven years building a small business, pouring his evenings and savings into it, and watched it fail in one bad year he couldn't have prevented. He has come to the study quietly convinced the failure was a verdict: if he'd been more faithful or more gifted, or more favored by God, the business would have stood.

Use his story to test the doctrine of the curse. Ask the group whether the ground sometimes resists the hand no matter how good the hand is, whether thorns come up in fields that were planted right. Help him hear that the collapse of honest work isn't always a judgment on the worker, that even diligent labor can come to nothing through no sin of the laborer, and that Ecclesiastes named this grief long before he felt it.

Then ask the harder question. Where is the line between the curse he couldn't control and the choices he could, and how does being truthful about both keep him from false guilt and from false innocence? Let the group sit in that tension without resolving it too quickly. If his loss has left him in real distress, talk with him privately afterward.

memoryVerse.text: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken.

sessions.title: The Lie That Splits the World
sessions.aim: To take apart the lie that ministry is holy work and everything else is secular and second-class, to recover the doctrine of vocation, and to hear from Luther and Dorothy Sayers that the farmer's and the carpenter's work pleases God as fully as the priest's.
sessions.summary:
There's a lie so deep in the church that most believers don't know they hold it. It says some work is sacred and some is secular: the pastor and the missionary do God's work, the plumber and the accountant just do their jobs, and the closer your work is to a church building, the more it counts.

Scripture knows no such division. Paul writes to ordinary workers, many of them slaves, "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men" (Colossians 3:23). There is something true in the claim that ministry matters more: the gospel does carry eternal weight. But the conclusion doesn't follow, because God doesn't need a special religious category of work in order to be pleased. Martin Luther took the word vocation, which the medieval church had kept for monks, priests and nuns, and gave it back to the farmer, the magistrate and the mother. In the image his interpreters later used, God milks the cows through the milkmaid, feeding the world through ordinary hands. Dorothy Sayers asked why the church never tells a carpenter that the first thing his religion asks of him is to make good tables.

Then the turn, and it cuts toward the pastor first. If all honest work is holy, the pastor's work isn't more holy, only differently assigned. The moment a minister thinks his position makes his labor count more to God than the work of the woman who cleans the church, he has joined the very lie the gospel came to destroy.

keyScripture.why: "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men" (Colossians 3:23). Paul wrote it to ordinary workers, and the verses around it are addressed to slaves. It refuses any split between sacred and secular work and makes every honest task an offering to the Lord.

discussion.q: Somewhere underneath, have you believed that a pastor or a missionary is doing more important work for God than you are in your ordinary job? Where did that belief come from?
discussion.behind: Bring the lie into view before naming it. Most people carry the sacred-secular split without examining it, and it makes them feel their daily work is spiritually beside the point. Get the assumption into the open so it can be challenged. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Luther taught that God provides for the world through ordinary work; his interpreters put it as God milking the cows through the milkmaid. What changes when you picture God working through your job to care for your neighbors, rather than waiting for you at church?
discussion.behind: We imagine God present in religious work and absent from secular work. Help the room move God into the ordinary task, so people see their labor as one of the means by which God himself provides for the world. That gives dignity to the dullest job.

discussion.q: Dorothy Sayers asked why the church never tells a carpenter that the first demand of his religion is that he make good tables. Where has your faith stayed in the "spiritual" part of your life and never reached the quality and ethics of your daily work?
discussion.behind: Press on the gap Sayers names. Many people separate their faith from their craft, as if God cared about their devotional life but not their workmanship. Connect faith directly to the excellence and integrity of the work itself. The good table is a matter of religion.

discussion.q: If all honest work is holy to God, what does that do to the way you've ranked jobs, your own included, as more or less spiritual? What might change in how you treat people in unglamorous work?
discussion.behind: Move from self to neighbor. The lie doesn't only shrink our own work; it lets us look down on other people's. Take the ranking apart, so the room honors the janitor, the nurse and the farmer as doing work God values, and stops envying the platform jobs.

discussion.q: Pastors are tempted to believe their work counts more to God than the work of the people in their churches. Where do you sort your own life into work that counts and work that doesn't?
discussion.behind: Close by bringing everyone inside, and notice that the teaching turns on the professional Christian first. Everyone ranks their hours into the meaningful and the meaningless. Invite people to find where they do it, and go first. The aim is to end the ranking, in the leader's heart first.

objections.objection: Surely ministry really is more important than secular work. Preaching the gospel deals with eternity, and fixing a sink doesn't. You can't seriously claim a plumber's work matters to God as much as a missionary's.
objections.response: Part of this is true. The proclamation of the gospel does deal with eternal things, and it would be foolish to flatten every difference between tasks. But the conclusion doesn't follow. The question isn't which work has the most visible eternal content. It's what pleases God, and God is pleased by obedience and love offered through honest labor, whatever the labor is. He doesn't need a special religious category to be glorified. The plumber who fixes the sink so a family has clean water, doing it as for the Lord and in love for that family, is doing work God receives as fully as the missionary's sermon. Luther saw this: God feeds, governs and heals the world through the farmer, the magistrate and the physician. The gospel is supreme in its message. It doesn't create a caste system of holy and unholy jobs.

objections.objection: If every job is equally holy, why does it matter what I do at all? This just lets people stay in selfish, even harmful work and call it their calling. It erases any real difference between vocations.
objections.response: No, and the doctrine of vocation has a sharp edge here. Saying all honest work is holy doesn't mean all work is honest. The con artist, the predatory lender and the maker of what destroys his neighbor have no vocation in the Christian sense, because vocation is measured by love of neighbor, by work that serves rather than exploits. Lester DeKoster argued that work is how we make ourselves useful to others, so work that harms rather than serves fails the very test of vocation. And within honest work, the doctrine doesn't erase the difference between doing the job well and doing it badly, faithfully or corruptly. What it erases is the false ranking of jobs by their distance from a church building. It honors the honest plumber. It doesn't bless the dishonest one, and it presses every worker in every field toward the love of neighbor and integrity that make work an offering God can receive.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you really believed God was working through your ordinary job to love your neighbors and provide for the world, what's one thing you'd do differently at work tomorrow?
sessions.practice: This week, take the part of your job you've most quietly considered unspiritual and do it the way Sayers said: aim to make a good table. Whatever your version of a good table is, the well-kept books, the clean room, the patient phone call, the careful repair, do that one thing with the deliberate intention that its excellence is an offering to God and an act of love for your neighbor. Write down whether treating the craft itself as worship changed the work.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you feed the world through the work of ordinary hands, and we've insulted you by dividing our days into holy hours and secular ones, as if you were present only in church. Forgive us for ranking your callings, for envying the platform and despising the workbench. Forgive those of us in the work of ministry most of all, for the pride that made our labor count more in our own eyes than the labor of your people. Teach us that all honest work done for you is holy, and send us back to our jobs as priests of the ordinary, to make good tables for your glory. Amen.
reflection: Where have I divided my life into work that counts to God and work that doesn't, and what would it mean to offer him the whole of it?
If God works through my job to provide for my neighbors, who exactly are the neighbors my work serves, and have I ever seen my labor as love for them?
Whose work have I quietly looked down on as less spiritual than my own, and what does that ranking show about the lie I've absorbed?
sessions.teaching:
There's a lie buried so deep in the soil of the church that most believers have never dug it up to look at it, and it quietly poisons how they think about the forty hours that fill their week. The lie is that some work is sacred and some is secular. The pastor, the missionary, the worship leader and the seminary professor do God's work. The plumber, the accountant, the line cook, the schoolteacher and the parent at home do mere jobs. The closer your work sits to a church building or a Bible, the more it counts to God, and the further out it sits, into the ordinary economy of the world, the more it shrinks into something God merely tolerates until you come back inside on Sunday. If you've ever felt your job was spiritually beside the point, that God's real mission was happening somewhere else and you were just funding it, you've felt the weight of this lie. So we're going to take it out and break it.

Start with Scripture, because Scripture doesn't know this division. When Paul writes, "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men" (Colossians 3:23), he isn't writing to clergy. He's writing to ordinary believers, and the sentence sits in a passage addressed to bondservants, people doing some of the most menial work imaginable. He tells them, "You are serving the Lord Christ" (Colossians 3:24). We should be clear that Paul isn't blessing the institution of slavery here; he's telling people who had almost no control over their work that even that work was done for Christ and seen by him. There's no exception clause for dull jobs or secular jobs or jobs that don't feel religious. "Whatever you do." Elsewhere he says it again: "whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). The whole daily grind is handed back to the worker as an offering made directly to God.

Now take the objection at its strongest, because every serious Christian feels it. Surely ministry is more important. Preaching the gospel touches eternity; fixing a sink doesn't. How can the plumber's work matter to God as much as the missionary's? There's something true here, and I don't want to flatten it. The eternal weight of the gospel is real, and not every task carries the same visible eternal content. But watch the conclusion fail to follow. The question isn't which job has the most obvious religious content. It's what pleases God, and what pleases God is obedience and love offered through honest work, whatever the work happens to be.

This was Martin Luther's great recovery, and the church has been forgetting it ever since. The medieval church had kept the word vocation, calling, for the monk, the priest and the nun, the so-called religious life. Luther opened it up. In his 1520 address To the Christian Nobility he argued that the shoemaker, the smith and the farmer each have the work and office of their trade from God, as truly as any priest. God calls the farmer to farm, the magistrate to govern and the mother to mother, and these callings are as holy as the call to preach. Later interpreters of Luther, the Swedish scholar Gustaf Wingren among them, summed up his teaching with a homely picture: God milks the cows through the milkmaid. God feeds the world, but he doesn't rain bread from the sky. He feeds it through the farmer who grows the grain, the baker who bakes it, the driver who hauls it and the cashier who sells it. Your job, however ordinary, is one of the ways God's providing hand reaches into the world to care for your neighbors. You aren't on the sidelines of God's work. You're one of the means of it.

Scripture has hints of this all through it. The first person the Bible names as "filled... with the Spirit of God" is Bezalel, a craftsman, given skill "to work in gold, silver, and bronze... and in carving wood, to work in every craft" (Exodus 31:3-5). Joseph served in a pagan household, and "his master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD caused all that he did to succeed in his hands" (Genesis 39:3).

Dorothy Sayers sharpened the point in her 1942 address Why Work?, and her question should sting every one of us. She observed that the church's approach to a carpenter was usually to tell him to stay sober and come to church on Sundays, and she argued that what the church ought to tell him is that the very first demand his religion makes on him is that he make good tables. The integrity and excellence of the work itself is a matter of religion, not a secular thing happening alongside his faith. A carpenter serves God by carpentry, by making a table that's true and strong and well joined, and a Christian carpenter who makes shoddy tables while keeping his devotions has missed the point. The work is meant to be worship.

And now the turn, and I have to take it standing where it cuts deepest, because I'm the professional Christian here, the man in the pulpit, the one this lie flatters most. If all honest work is holy, the pastor's work isn't more holy than the work of the people in the pews. It's differently assigned, not more valuable. Pastors are tempted not to believe that in their bones. It's easy to stand up front and quietly feel that the preaching, praying and counseling count to God in a way the work of the person who cleans the building after everyone leaves doesn't. That's the lie in its purest and ugliest form, dressed for church. The gospel didn't come to build a caste system of sacred and secular jobs with clergy on top. It came to tear that wall down, to make every believer part of "a royal priesthood" (1 Peter 2:9) and every honest task an altar. The moment I think my work matters more to God because it happens in a church, I've rejoined the very lie Christ died to destroy.

So let it reach the place where you've been ranking your hours. There's no secular work for the Christian, only work done with God or without him. The farmer and the missionary, the carpenter and the pastor, the spreadsheet and the sermon, done heartily as for the Lord, are holy. Go make good tables.

scriptureStudy.note: "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward." Written to ordinary workers and slaves, not clergy, it refuses any sacred-secular split and makes all honest labor an offering to Christ.

"So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." God's glory isn't confined to religious acts. It reaches the whole of ordinary life, so no part of work falls outside worship.

"I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship... to work in every craft." The first person Scripture names as filled with the Spirit of God is a craftsman, and the filling is for skilled work.
"But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood." The priesthood belongs to all believers, not a clerical class, so every Christian offers his whole life, work included, as priestly service.

"Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him." Paul roots calling in God's assignment, so an ordinary station and an ordinary job are themselves a place of calling, not a holding pattern.

"Rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man." Even constrained labor is reframed as service to Christ, who receives the work directly. (Paul isn't endorsing slavery; he's telling the powerless that their work is seen.)

"His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD caused all that he did to succeed in his hands." Joseph serves God through faithful, excellent work in a pagan household, and God is present in that ordinary labor.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at how the church split the world in two, because the sacred-secular divide didn't fall from heaven. It was built over centuries, and it can be taken down. In the medieval church a sharp line ran between the religious life, monks, nuns and clergy, who were thought to have a true vocation, and the laity in their ordinary trades, who were permitted a lower station while the spiritual elite pursued the higher way. Luther broke this open in the Reformation, insisting that the plowman and the magistrate have callings as real as any monk's, and that God works through ordinary stations to govern and provide for the world.

Set this beside the modern secular version of the same split, where work is divided into meaningful careers that supposedly express your true self and mere jobs you endure for money. It's a new caste system, and it crushes the worker in ordinary labor just as the old one did. Ask how deeply each division has shaped your group. Os Guinness, in The Call (1998), distinguishes our primary calling, to God himself, from our secondary callings to particular work and stations, and warns both against collapsing all of life into work and against dismissing ordinary work as spiritually empty. Gene Edward Veith's God at Work and Sayers's Why Work? are good companions for this session.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose two people in the same group name their work in the same week. The first is a young woman headed to the mission field, and the room lights up, prays over her and takes up a collection. The second is a man who installs heating systems, and when he says so, the room nods politely and moves on. He notices. He always notices.

Ask the group, gently and directly, why the room responded the way it did, and what the difference shows about the lie they've absorbed. Then walk the heating installer's work through the doctrine of vocation. In a Michigan winter he's the reason families don't freeze, one of the hands through which God keeps the vulnerable warm. His work is no less holy than the missionary's, only differently assigned. The aim isn't to diminish the missionary but to lift the installer, and to help the room repent of a ranking it didn't know it was keeping. End by asking each person whose ordinary work they've quietly counted as lesser.
