sessions.title: When Work Becomes a God
sessions.aim: To name the idol ordinary work becomes when it stops being what we do and starts being who we are, to expose the anxiety of a life built on production, and to set God's rest against the lie that we are what we achieve.
sessions.summary:
Work was a gift, then it was cursed, then the church split it in two. Now we come to the deepest danger, which isn't that we'll despise our work but that we'll worship it. Good things make the most dangerous gods, and work is a very good thing, which is exactly why it makes such a ruinous idol.

What happens when work stops being something you do and becomes what you are, when your job isn't your calling but your identity, the place you go to prove you exist and earn the right to be loved? Ambition has a real defense. Scripture praises the diligent and rebukes the sluggard, and excellence honors God. The problem isn't working hard. It's what we're chasing when we work too hard. Underneath the long hours there's often a hunger for a verdict: the need to hear from the boss or the market or the voice in our head that we're enough, that we've earned our place. Work was never strong enough to carry that, and was never meant to.

The turn falls on the pastor first. The minister who works himself to exhaustion for the kingdom and calls it faithfulness, who can't rest because the church might fail without him, has made an idol of the work of God, and the Sabbath command stands against him as much as against the workaholic banker. "Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God" (Exodus 20:9-10). God's rest isn't laziness; it's the weekly declaration that the world runs without us, because we aren't God.

keyScripture.why: "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work" (Exodus 20:8-10). The weekly stop breaks the tyranny of production and declares that our worth, and the world's survival, don't rest on our work.

discussion.q: When someone asks who you are, how quickly do you answer with what you do for a living? What does that tell you about how tightly your identity is tied to your job?
discussion.behind: Start with a simple, revealing habit. Most of us define ourselves by our work without noticing. Bring out how much of our sense of self is built on our job before naming it an idol, so the room feels the grip before judging it. Go first.

discussion.q: The problem isn't working hard but what we're chasing when we work too hard. What do you think you're after underneath your hardest work: a verdict, a sense of worth, a love you're trying to earn?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. Press past the surface of ambition to the hunger beneath it, and help people recognize that overwork is often a search for a verdict that they're enough. Keep it tender. Many in the room are exhausted from chasing exactly this. Go first.

discussion.q: Good things make the most dangerous gods, and work is a very good thing. How have you seen the goodness of your work become the very reason it took over your life?
discussion.behind: We expect idols to be obvious vices, but the strongest idols are good gifts loved too much. Help the room see that the dignity of work, which session 1 established, is exactly what makes it so easy to worship, so they stop looking for the idol in the wrong place.

discussion.q: Read Exodus 20:8-11 and Deuteronomy 5:12-15. Underneath the Sabbath command is the claim that the world runs without you, because you aren't God. Why is it so hard for you to actually stop, and what does that difficulty show?
discussion.behind: For most of us, refusing to stop isn't commitment but fear: the dread that everything falls apart without us. Bring out the working belief that we're holding the world together, which the Sabbath exists to break. Help people feel both the pride and the anxiety in the refusal to rest. Be gentle with anyone whose long hours come from need, not pride.

discussion.q: Pastors and church workers can work themselves to exhaustion for the church and call it faithfulness, when really they can't bear to find out whether the work needs them. Where have you dressed up your own overwork as virtue, and what fear was underneath?
discussion.behind: Close by bringing everyone inside, and notice that the teaching names the religious workaholic first. The point is to see how we sanctify our idolatry of work as diligence or devotion. Invite people to find the fear under their busyness, and go first. The aim is truth, not more guilt.

objections.objection: There's nothing wrong with ambition. The Bible praises the diligent and rebukes the sluggard, excellence honors God, and hard work is a virtue. You're just making people feel guilty for being good at their jobs.
objections.response: All of that is true, and the study has no quarrel with it. Scripture praises diligence and rebukes laziness, excellence honors God, and the earlier sessions argued that work is a good gift to be done heartily. Working hard isn't the sin. So hear the distinction carefully, because it's the whole point. The question isn't whether you work hard but what you're working for, what you're chasing underneath the hours. Ambition becomes idolatry not when it's strong but when the work stops being something you do and becomes the thing that tells you whether you're worth anything. The diligent worker the Bible praises can rest on the seventh day, because his worth doesn't depend on his output. The idolater can't stop, because stopping means facing whether he's anything at all without the work. The issue isn't the effort. It's whether work has become the god you go to for a verdict on your soul.

objections.objection: If I stop working so hard, I'll fall behind, lose my job, fail my family. Telling me to rest and not find my identity in work is a luxury for people who can afford it. Some of us have to grind just to survive.
objections.response: Treat this gently, because it's the most painful objection in the room and it's often true. Many people work long and hard not out of idolatry but out of necessity, to feed children and keep a roof overhead, and this study must never shame someone grinding to survive as if their labor were a spiritual failure. That labor is honorable, and the Sabbath was given by a God who knows the difference between a worker crushed by need and a worker driven by pride. But notice who first received the command. "You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt... Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day" (Deuteronomy 5:15). It was given to former slaves, people who had known forced, ceaseless labor, and it came as liberation, a right to stop that no Egyptian master had ever granted. Even under real pressure, the question underneath remains: does my survival rest finally on my own effort, or on the God who feeds the birds? Rest isn't always a luxury. Sometimes it's the hardest act of faith a tired person can make.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your work were taken from you tomorrow, the job, the title, the productivity, who would you be? Does the answer frighten you?
sessions.practice: This week, take one full block of time, an evening, a morning, ideally a whole day, and stop working entirely. No email, no catching up, no productive hobby disguised as rest. Just stop, on purpose. When the anxiety rises that you're falling behind or that things will fall apart, say out loud that the world is held together by God and not by you. Write down how hard it was to stop and what the difficulty taught you about what you've been worshiping. If your circumstances truly won't allow a whole day, take the hour you can.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we've taken the good gift of work and made it a god, and we've knelt at the altar of our own production, trying to earn a verdict that we're enough, a worth you offered us free in Christ. Forgive us. Forgive those of us who have worked ourselves to exhaustion even for your church and called the idolatry faithfulness. Teach us to stop, to keep the Sabbath, to declare with our rest that the world runs without us because you never needed us to hold it together. Free us from the lie that we are what we achieve. We're yours, loved before we ever worked a day. Let us rest in that. Amen.
reflection: What verdict am I trying to earn through my work, and from whom, and what would change if I believed that verdict had already been spoken over me in Christ?
Where has the goodness of my work become the reason it has taken over my life?
Why is it so hard for me to stop and rest, and what does that show about whether I believe the world depends on me or on God?
sessions.teaching:
We've followed work through three movements. It was a gift in the garden. It was cursed in the fall. And the church split it into a sacred tier and a secular one, a lie we spent last week tearing down. Now we come to the most dangerous turn, because the deepest threat to your soul isn't that you'll despise your work. It's that you'll worship it.

We usually get idolatry wrong. We expect our idols to be obvious vices, the bottle, the affair, the greed we can name and confess. But the most dangerous gods aren't bad things. They're good things loved too much, asked to carry a weight they were never built to bear. And work is a very good thing. We've spent three sessions establishing how good, how dignified, how God-given it is, which is exactly what makes it such a ruinous idol. You don't build an altar to something you despise. You build it to something you love.

Here's the question that exposes it. What happens when your work stops being something you do and quietly becomes what you are? When your job isn't your calling but your identity? When the first thing you reach for when a stranger asks who you are is what you do for a living, because underneath you suspect that what you do is what you are, and if the doing stopped, the being would stop with it? That's the idol. It's the moment work becomes the place you go to prove you exist, to earn the right to take up space.

Take the objection at full strength, because the Bible is on its side. There's nothing wrong with ambition. "The soul of the diligent is richly supplied" (Proverbs 13:4). Excellence honors God, and we've argued for two sessions that work should be done heartily, as for the Lord. So am I going to make people feel guilty for being good at their jobs? No. Working hard isn't the sin. The distinction is everything. The question isn't whether you work hard. It's what you're working for. What are you chasing, underneath the long hours and the late nights and the inability to stop?

For most of us, if we're truthful, it isn't finally the work itself. It's a verdict. We're working to hear something, from the boss, the market, the numbers, the parent in our head who was never satisfied, the silent crowd we keep trying to impress. We're working to hear that we're enough, that we've earned our place, that we're worth keeping. The Preacher saw it long ago: "all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind" (Ecclesiastes 4:4). We're trying to justify our existence by our production, and that's the idol in its essence: using work to do what only the gospel can do, to answer whether we're loved and allowed to be here. Work can't bear that weight, so it crushes us. The promotion satisfies for a week and then the bar moves. The achievement that was going to settle the question settles nothing, and we're off after the next one, more anxious than before, because an idol always demands more and never gives what it promised. Jesus told of a man who built bigger barns and said to his soul, relax, and heard God say, "Fool! This night your soul is required of you" (Luke 12:20).

The cure God built into the structure of the week is the one we resist most. "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work" (Exodus 20:8-10). The Sabbath isn't a command to be lazy. It's more confrontational than that. It's the weekly act of stopping your work in order to declare, with your body and your calendar, that the world doesn't depend on you. It keeps turning when you stop. The harvest comes, the bills get handled, the church stands, the company survives, because you're a creature and not the Creator, and you were never the one holding it together. "It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep" (Psalm 127:2).

That's why we find it so hard to stop. The difficulty is the diagnosis. If you can't rest, somewhere down deep you believe that everything falls apart without you, which is to believe you're God, the load-bearing wall of your own small universe. The Sabbath calls the bluff. It makes you lay the work down and find out, every week, that the world held without you.

Pastors are chief sinners here, because they can hide this idolatry under the holiest disguise there is, the work of God itself. It's easy to work yourself to exhaustion for the church and call it faithfulness: skip the rest, answer the email at midnight, carry the whole congregation in your chest like a stone you can't set down, and tell yourself it's devotion. It isn't, or not only. Underneath, the truth is simpler and uglier. The worker can't bear to find out whether the work needs him. He needs to be needed, because if the church runs fine without him, he has to face who he is when he isn't producing for God, and that question frightens him. The minister who can't rest because the kingdom might fail without him has made an idol of the work of God, the most respectable idol in the world and one of the deadliest. The Sabbath command stands over me exactly as it stands over the banker who lives at his desk.

So hear the word a tired, driven soul most needs. You aren't what you achieve. The verdict you're working so hard to earn has already been spoken over you, free, in Christ, who loved you and called you his own before you produced a thing. You can stop now. Not because the work doesn't matter, but because your worth was never in it. Lay it down one day in seven and discover that the God who feeds the birds was holding the world the whole time, and holding you.

scriptureStudy.note: "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God." The command to stop one day in seven breaks the tyranny of endless production and declares that our worth, and the world, don't rest on our work.

"You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt... Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day." Rest is rooted in liberation from slavery: a God-given right to stop that Egypt's ceaseless economy never granted.

"Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" The rich man stores up bigger barns. Jesus exposes the idol of production and accumulation in a man whose whole identity was what he'd gathered.

"Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity." The Preacher names the hidden engine under much ambition: rivalry, and the restless hunger for a verdict.
"You cannot serve God and money." Jesus names wealth, and the work we do to gain it, as a rival god demanding service. Whatever we serve for our security and identity becomes our master.

"Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain... It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep." The psalm confronts the anxiety of overwork directly, and ends in the gift of sleep.
"For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" Jesus weighs the soul against all the world's achievement and calls the trade a catastrophic loss.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, think about the idea that idolatry is rarely the worship of obvious evils and almost always the worship of good things asked to be God, because that's the key to seeing how work, the gift, becomes work, the idol. The prophets railed against idols of wood and stone, but writers across the tradition have drawn out the deeper diagnosis: the human heart keeps taking good gifts and making ultimate things of them, demanding that a career or a family or a reputation give the security and worth only God can give. Tim Keller, in Counterfeit Gods (2009) and again in Every Good Endeavor, argues that work is among the most common and respectable idols, and that because it can't bear that weight it ends either in crushing anxiety when we fail or empty restlessness when we succeed.

Set that beside a culture in which "Who are you?" is answered by "What do you do?" and rest is treated as falling behind, and ask how thoroughly that culture has discipled your group. Weigh the Sabbath not as an outdated rule but as a frontal challenge to the idol of production. Then read Hebrews 4:9-10: "there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God's rest has also rested from his works as God did from his." That rest gathers up the whole theme: a ceasing not only from labor but from the striving to justify ourselves, received as a gift.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is succeeding by every outward measure: promotion, title, income, the respect of his field. And he can't sleep, can't stop checking his phone at dinner, can't sit through a family vacation without a low hum of dread that someone is getting ahead while he rests. He tells the group he doesn't know who he'd be if he stopped, and that the not knowing scares him more than the exhaustion.

Handle him without flattery and without contempt, because his idol has been applauded his whole life. Ask the group what verdict he's working to hear, and from whom, and why no promotion has ever quieted the question for more than a week. Then bring the Sabbath to bear. Ask him, and the room, what it would cost to stop for one full day and find out whether the world held together without him. The aim isn't to shame the achiever. It's to show him that what he's chasing through work was already given to him free in Christ, and that his inability to rest is the clearest sign he hasn't yet believed it. If the sleeplessness and dread sound like more than a bad season, encourage him privately to talk with a doctor or counselor as well.

memoryVerse.text: Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.

sessions.title: Our Labor Is Not in Vain
sessions.aim: To bring the study to its hope: our work is taken up into the kingdom and not lost, excellence done in love is a form of worship, and in the new creation the work of our hands is redeemed, not abolished.
sessions.summary:
The study has gone down into the garden, the curse, the lie and the idol. Now it has to come up into hope, because the gospel doesn't leave work in the thorns or on the ash heap of vanity. This session gathers everything toward one remarkable claim: "in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Start with what redeemed work is at ground level. Lester DeKoster put it simply: work is how we make ourselves useful to others. To work well is to love the world through the things our hands make and the services they give, an act of love and not merely a transaction.

The strongest objection is that it all burns: nothing we build down here lasts, so it can't finally matter. There is a real judgment in Scripture, and a real purging. But the Bible's picture of the end isn't annihilation followed by a disembodied heaven. N. T. Wright has worked to recover what the church half forgot: the future is resurrection and a new heavens and a new earth, and into the city "they will bring... the glory and the honor of the nations" (Revelation 21:26). Paul ends his great chapter on the resurrection not in the clouds but at the workbench. The faithful work that seemed to vanish, the good table no one praised, the years of service no one saw, the cup of cold water, isn't lost. So we work, not to earn and not to justify ourselves, but as people who know the Monday they're living matters into eternity.

keyScripture.why: "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58). Paul ends the Bible's great chapter on the resurrection with a word about work, and promises that faithful labor isn't lost.

discussion.q: Lester DeKoster said work is how we make ourselves useful to others, a form of love. Whose lives does your work actually touch and serve, and have you ever thought of your job as a way of loving them?
discussion.behind: Gather the study toward love of neighbor. Most people see work as a transaction, not an act of love. Help them trace the actual people their work serves, the people fed, helped, healed or taught, so the daily grind shows up again as love made practical. Go first.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 15:50-58. Paul ends the great resurrection chapter not with heaven but with work: your labor is not in vain. Why do you think he puts the deepest hope in the Bible next to a command about your work, and how does that change how Monday feels?
discussion.behind: We expect resurrection to point us away from earthly work. Instead Paul points us back to it. Let the room feel that the resurrection makes work matter more, not less, because nothing done in the Lord is finally lost.

discussion.q: Read Revelation 21:22-27. Some say it all burns, so nothing we build lasts. How does the promise of a new creation, an earth renewed rather than discarded, answer that despair?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The fire and the judgment are real, and no one should leave with a naive optimism. But the end is renewal, not annihilation, an earth made new into which the good of human labor is carried. Help people see the difference between everything being destroyed and everything being purified and redeemed.

discussion.q: If excellence done in love is a form of worship, what would it mean to treat the quality of your work this week as an offering to God, rather than just a way to keep your job?
discussion.behind: Move to the practical. Connect the high theology of redeemed work to the concrete craft of the week, so doing the job well becomes worship and love, not mere duty. Help the room see the offering hidden in ordinary competence done for the right reasons.

discussion.q: Looking back over all five sessions, the gift, the curse, the lie, the idol and now the hope, what's the one thing you most need to believe about your work, and what has kept you from believing it until now?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study by bringing everyone inside, and don't resolve it neatly. Invite each person, the leader first, to name the truth they most need and what resists it. Send the room back to Monday carrying the hope, not setting the study down as finished.

objections.objection: It all burns in the end. Scripture says the earth and its works will be burned up and this world is passing away. Whatever I build down here, however good, is temporary and can't finally matter. Only souls last.
objections.response: The fire is in the Bible, and there's a real judgment and a real purging. The study won't trade that for a comfortable lie. But look harder at what the end is, because much of the church has half forgotten it. Even the verse usually quoted here, 2 Peter 3:10, reads in the ESV that "the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed," laid bare before God, not simply erased. The Bible doesn't promise annihilation followed by souls floating in a spiritual heaven. It promises resurrection and "a new heaven and a new earth" (Revelation 21:1), and into that city "they will bring... the glory and the honor of the nations" (Revelation 21:26). Paul describes the fire as a test: the Day "will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done" (1 Corinthians 3:13). It burns the wood, hay and straw and keeps the gold. And Paul doesn't end the resurrection chapter saying nothing matters. He ends it commanding work, because your labor in the Lord isn't in vain.

objections.objection: This makes Christians strive even harder, now with eternity riding on every task. Last week you warned against the idol of work, and now you're telling me my work echoes into eternity, which will just feed the workaholism all over again.
objections.response: It's a fair worry, and the study has to hold the two sessions together rather than let the fifth undo the fourth. The difference is the engine underneath. The idol of work, named last week, is work as the way we justify ourselves, earn our worth and prove we exist; it runs on fear and ends in exhaustion. Redeemed work is work as the overflow of a worth already given, an offering made by people who have already heard in Christ that they're enough, so it runs on gratitude, not fear. Knowing your labor isn't in vain doesn't mean it earns you anything, because Christ earned it all. It means the good you do out of love is kept and not wasted, which is freedom, not pressure. You don't work harder in order to be loved. You work well because you already are.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What faithful work have you done that seemed to vanish, the good no one saw or praised, and what would it mean to believe God has kept it and won't let it be lost?
sessions.practice: This week, do one piece of your work believing that it isn't in vain: that it's love for a real neighbor and an offering God keeps. Pick something small and ordinary and do it with both in mind: this serves someone, and this matters to God. Then name one neighbor your work serves and find a way to do that part especially well, as love. Write down what it was like to work as someone whose labor isn't lost.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you didn't abandon our work to the thorns or the fire. You took it up. You became a worker yourself, a carpenter, and you're making all things new, a renewed creation into which the good of our labor will be carried and kept. Forgive us for the years we thought it all meaningless, and for the years we made it everything. Free us to work now as people whose worth is already settled in you and whose labor isn't in vain. Let the work of our hands be love for our neighbors and worship of you, and keep what we offer, even the parts no one saw. We bring you our Mondays. Receive them. Amen.
reflection: Have I lived as if my work were finally meaningless, or as if it were everything, and what would it mean to hold the truth between them: it isn't in vain, and it isn't my god?
Whose lives does my work actually serve, and what would change if I did my job as an act of love for those particular neighbors?
What faithful work of mine has seemed to vanish unseen, and how does the promise that God keeps such work change the way I'll work tomorrow?
sessions.teaching:
We've taken work down a long road in this study. We started in the garden, where it was a gift, part of the image of a God who works. We followed it into the fall, where the ground turned against the hand and the thorns and sweat came in. We tore down the lie that splits work into sacred and secular, and we named the idol work becomes when we ask it to tell us who we are. If the study ended there, it would leave you where the culture leaves you, caught between the despair that says work is meaningless and the idolatry that says work is everything. The gospel refuses both, and this last session is where it says so. It gathers everything toward Paul's claim that "in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Start with what redeemed work is at ground level, because before we lift our eyes to eternity we have to see the neighbor in front of us. Lester DeKoster, in his short book Work: The Meaning of Your Life, put it as plainly as it can be put: work is how we make ourselves useful to others. Think about what that means. The farmer's labor becomes food on a stranger's table. The nurse's shift becomes the recovery of someone she'll never see again. The engineer's careful calculation becomes the bridge that carries a family home. The teacher's patience becomes a child's ability to read, decades from now. Work is the web by which God knits us into one another's service, so every honest job done well is a way of loving people, most of whom we'll never meet. Jesus said that "whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple... will by no means lose his reward" (Matthew 10:42), and that "as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me" (Matthew 25:40). Work that serves rather than exploits is love made concrete, love of neighbor with a paycheck attached.

That alone would give it dignity. But Paul goes further, and we have to follow him into the strongest objection there is. It all burns, doesn't it? This world is passing away, and only souls last. There are verses about fire and judgment and the dissolving of the present order, and I won't pretend them away. There is a real judgment and a real purging. Grant the fire. But much of the church has absorbed a picture that owes more to Plato than to Scripture: the material world thrown away and disembodied souls drifting off to a spiritual heaven. That isn't the Bible's hope. N. T. Wright has spent years recovering what the church half forgot, especially in Surprised by Hope (2008): the Christian hope is resurrection, the body raised, and a new heavens and a new earth. Not the scrapping of creation but its renewal. "The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption" (Romans 8:21).

And listen to what Revelation says is carried into that city: "the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it... They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations" (Revelation 21:24, 26). The good fruit of human culture and labor, purified, is carried in. The fire Paul describes isn't annihilation. It's a test. The Day of judgment "will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done" (1 Corinthians 3:13). It burns the wood, hay and straw and keeps the gold, silver and precious stones.

Now watch where Paul lands the greatest chapter ever written on the resurrection. 1 Corinthians 15 is the towering argument that Christ is risen and we will rise, that "Death is swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54). After all that height, you'd expect him to say, therefore set your minds on heaven and despise this passing world. He says the opposite. "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain." The resurrection doesn't make work meaningless. It makes it matter forever. Because Christ is raised and creation will be renewed, the good you do now isn't poured into a void. In a way Paul doesn't fully explain and we can't fully see, the faithful labor of your hands is taken up and kept in the world God is making new. "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord... that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!" (Revelation 14:13).

Hear this where it lands hardest, in the places where your work seems to have vanished without a trace. The good table no one praised. The years you served in a role no one saw. The faithful, unglamorous labor that produced no monument and was forgotten by everyone but you. A parent's ten thousand unseen acts of care. The believer who did a secular job with quiet integrity for forty years and wondered whether any of it mattered to God. None of it is lost. Not one cup of cold water. God has kept it.

So we come to the end, and this study doesn't resolve so much as lift. Work this side of the new creation is still mixed with thorns, still tempted toward the idol, still hard on a Monday morning, and the study doesn't promise the grind will disappear before Christ returns. What it changes is the meaning of the grind. You work now not to justify yourself, because Christ has already justified you, and not in despair that it's all vanity, because your labor isn't in vain. You work as someone who has heard the verdict and been set free by it, offering the excellence of your hands as worship and their usefulness as love. So go back to your work. Make the good table, serve the neighbor, do it heartily, as for the Lord. And when it feels small and forgotten, remember the last word of the great resurrection chapter, spoken to workers exactly like you. Your labor is not in vain.

scriptureStudy.note: "Be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain." Paul ends the resurrection chapter with work, grounding the worth of daily labor in the resurrection, so nothing done in the Lord is finally lost.

"The kings of the earth will bring their glory into it... They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations." The good fruit of human culture and labor is carried into the new Jerusalem, taken up into the renewed creation rather than discarded.

"Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on... that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!" The faithful works of God's people aren't left behind at death. They follow them, kept by God.

"As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me." Jesus receives our service to our neighbors as service to himself, so ordinary work that helps real people is love offered to Christ and seen by him.

"Knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ." The reward for faithful work comes from the Lord himself, which assures the worker that unseen and unrewarded labor is received.

"The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God." The cursed creation of session 2 is promised freedom: the material world renewed, not thrown away.

"For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them." We're God's own handiwork, made for works he has already prepared, so our labor is woven into his purpose.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at the recovery of the doctrine of the new creation, because the worth of our work finally rests on what we believe about the end, and the church has often believed the wrong thing. For long stretches popular Christianity absorbed a vision more indebted to Plato than to Scripture, in which the material world is a disposable shell, the body a prison and salvation the soul's escape to a non-physical heaven. That vision drains all lasting significance from physical work and earthly culture. N. T. Wright, especially in Surprised by Hope, argues for the biblical picture: bodily resurrection and renewed heavens and earth, God redeeming creation rather than scrapping it. If the end is annihilation, building anything is rearranging deck chairs. If the end is renewal, the good we build in love is somehow taken up and kept.

Set this beside Keller's argument in Every Good Endeavor that our work takes part in God's own work of cultivating and restoring the world, and that the gospel frames work as neither salvation nor futility but service. Then weigh how the fire of judgment works in 1 Corinthians 3:10-15: not the destruction of all earthly work, but a refining that burns away what was done in vanity and pride and keeps what was done in love. Hold the whole arc of the study together: work given in Eden, frustrated by the fall, dignified in every vocation, guarded against idolatry, finds its end not on the ash heap but in the new creation.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose an older man in your group has recently retired after forty years of unremarkable work as a regional manager at a company most people have never heard of. He's quietly grieving, not the income but the suspicion that none of it mattered. There's no monument. No one will remember the spreadsheets, the meetings, the patient handling of difficult employees, the thousand small decisions made with integrity that no one saw.

Ask the group to trace whom his decades of faithful, ordinary work actually served: the employees whose livelihoods he protected, the families fed by a company he helped keep honest, the younger workers he shaped without ever calling it discipleship. Then bring 1 Corinthians 15:58 to bear on his grief. His labor, done in the Lord, isn't erased but kept, the cup of cold water multiplied across forty years. Let him, and everyone facing the same fear, hear that God has kept the good work no one remembered, and that the unseen faithfulness of an ordinary life is exactly the kind of labor that isn't in vain.

memoryVerse.text: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

leaderPrimer:
Your group will arrive at this study straight from the thing it studies, and they'll arrive tired. Whatever evening you meet, the room has already worked that day, and some of them half suspect the next five weeks will be one more demand dressed in Bible verses: a program to make their job spiritual on top of making it profitable, a second shift for the soul. Take that suspicion seriously early, because it isn't paranoia. The church has done this before, turning every doctrine into an assignment, and a study that convinces an exhausted man his data entry must now also be worship, performed with excellence and the right heart, has added a boss instead of removing one. The doctrine of vocation isn't a demand. It's a dignity. It says the work he already did today mattered to God before anyone told him to feel differently about it, and the study exists to hand that dignity back, not to send a bill for it.

Watch the edges of the room while you teach the center. Someone there is out of work, and every sentence about the goodness of work lands on their shame. Someone is retired and wondering whether they still count. Someone hates a job they can't leave, and the last thing they can bear is being told to find their passion. The study refuses that lie, and refuses its opposite, the idol that makes the job a self, and both refusals need your voice every week. If someone's exhaustion, job loss or sense of failure sounds like more than a hard season, if they speak of hopelessness or of not wanting to go on, talk with them privately that night, help them reach a pastor, counselor or doctor, and point them to the Find Help page on this site.

The teaching names the idol of work from inside the pastorate, a job easily loved into a god and worked at in order to avoid the God it's supposedly for. Ministry isn't the exception to this study. It's the first example, and saying so out loud will free the room. Keep session 4 unhurried, because rest is the argument underneath everything else: worth received instead of produced. And end where the study ends, with Paul's promise that "in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58). Send them out under that sentence, not under a new to-do list. They brought enough of those in with them.

faq.q: Is this study going to tell me my ordinary job does not really matter to God?
faq.a: The opposite. Session 3 exists to take apart exactly that lie, the belief that ministry is sacred work and everything else is secular and second-class. Scripture knows no such division. God worked first and called it good, he gave Adam a job before the fall, and Paul tells ordinary workers, even slaves, that whatever they do is done for the Lord Christ (Colossians 3:23-24). The study draws on Luther, who taught that God provides for the world through ordinary callings (his interpreters put it as God milking the cows through the milkmaid), and on Dorothy Sayers, who argued that the first thing a carpenter's religion asks of him is good tables. If you've ever felt your work was spiritually beside the point, this study was written for you. There's no secular work for the Christian, only work done with God or without him.

faq.q: Does the study think ambition and hard work are wrong?
faq.a: No. Scripture praises the diligent and rebukes the sluggard, excellence honors God, and the study argues across several sessions that work is a good gift to be done heartily. Working hard isn't the sin. Session 4 draws the line carefully. The question isn't whether you work hard but what you're chasing underneath the hard work. Ambition becomes idolatry not when it's strong but when work stops being something you do and becomes the thing that tells you whether you're worth anything. The diligent worker the Bible praises can rest on the seventh day, because his worth doesn't depend on his output.

faq.q: Is work a curse or a gift? The Bible seems to say both.
faq.a: Both, and the order matters. Work was a gift first, given in the garden before the fall, part of bearing the image of a God who works and calls his work good. Then the fall cursed it, not by inventing work but by corrupting work that was already there, so the ground now resists the hand and thorns and sweat come mixed into the labor (Genesis 3:17-19). The study gives a session to each, because it refuses both the romantic who pretends work is always satisfying and the cynic who says it's only vanity. The curse is real, but it's the middle of the story, not the first word, which was good, or the last, which is the new creation.

faq.q: Why does the study keep talking about the pastor and ministry as a job that can become an idol?
faq.a: Because the teaching won't stand outside the problem it names. Ministry is work, and it can be loved into an idol more easily than most, because the busyness can be dressed up as faithfulness and the need to be needed can be called devotion. A pastor can work himself to exhaustion for the church and call it faithfulness, or quietly believe his position makes his labor count more to God than the labor of the people he serves. The point isn't to single out clergy but to show that no work, not even the work of God, is safe from becoming a god, and that the leader is inside the problem first. A study that pointed only at other people's jobs would change no one.

faq.q: What does it mean to say my work is a way of loving my neighbor?
faq.a: Lester DeKoster put it simply in Work: The Meaning of Your Life: work is how we make ourselves useful to others. Your labor becomes the food on a stranger's table, the recovery of a patient you'll never meet, the bridge that carries a family home, a child's ability to read decades from now. Work is the web by which God knits us into one another's service, so every honest job done well is love made concrete. Session 5 builds on this, and on Jesus' words that what we do for "the least of these" we do for him (Matthew 25:40), down to a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42). Even the most ordinary task touches real lives, and that service is seen by God.

faq.q: If I find my identity in my work, what is so wrong with that?
faq.a: In the end, everything, because work can't bear that weight and it will crush you. Session 4 names this directly. When work stops being something you do and becomes what you are, the place you go to prove you exist and earn the right to be loved, it has become an idol, and idols always demand more and never give what they promise. The achievement that was going to settle the question of your worth settles nothing, and you're off after the next one, more anxious than before. The gospel speaks a verdict over you that work never could: you're loved in Christ before you produce a thing. The Sabbath is God's weekly challenge to the idol, making you stop and discover that the world held together without you.

faq.q: What is the Sabbath really about, and is the study saying I have to keep it like the Old Testament?
faq.a: The study presents the Sabbath less as a rule to enforce and more as a gift and a confrontation. The command to stop one day in seven isn't God endorsing laziness. It's the weekly act of declaring, with your body and your calendar, that the world doesn't depend on you, because you're a creature and not the Creator. It was first given to former slaves as liberation (Deuteronomy 5:15). The study doesn't settle the finer debates among Christians about how the day should be kept. It presses the deeper point: a people who can't stop have made an idol of their own production.

faq.q: Does our work really last, or does it all burn up in the end?
faq.a: The study takes the fire seriously, because Scripture speaks of a real judgment. But much of the church has half forgotten the shape of the Christian hope. The end isn't annihilation followed by disembodied souls in a spiritual heaven. It's resurrection and "a new heaven and a new earth" (Revelation 21:1), creation renewed rather than discarded, a hope N. T. Wright has worked to recover in Surprised by Hope. Revelation pictures the nations bringing their glory and honor into the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24-26). Paul describes the fire as a test that burns away what was worthless and keeps what lasts (1 Corinthians 3:12-15). And he ends the resurrection chapter with work: "in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58).

faq.q: I am stuck in a job I find meaningless. What does this study have for me?
faq.a: More than you might expect. Session 1 says your work, however ordinary, is part of how you bear the image of a working God. Session 3 says there's no sacred caste of jobs, that the most routine labor done for the Lord is holy, and it asks you to see the neighbor your work serves. Session 5 promises that even faithful work that seems to vanish is kept by God. The study won't pretend a dull job is thrilling, because it refuses the lie that good work always feels good. But it won't let you believe your hours are spiritually empty either. If the job is doing you real harm, or the weight of it has become more than you can carry, tell your leader; this study doesn't ask anyone to stay in a place that's crushing them.

faq.q: Does the study promise that if I follow it I will finally love my job?
faq.a: No, and it deliberately refuses to. Session 5 lifts rather than resolves, because work this side of the new creation is still mixed with thorns, still tempted toward the idol, still hard on a Monday morning. The study doesn't promise the grind disappears before Christ returns. What it changes is the meaning of the grind. You work not to justify yourself, because Christ already has, and not in despair that it's all vanity, because your labor isn't in vain. The hope isn't a room of people who suddenly love their jobs but a room of people who've stopped despising their work and stopped worshiping it.

faq.q: I am retired, or unemployed, or unable to work. Does any of this apply to me?
faq.a: Yes, and the study keeps you in view. Its deepest claim cuts against the idol that ties your worth to your output, and that claim is for you most of all. If your value was never in your productivity, then losing a job, aging out of it or never being able to do it doesn't diminish who you are before God. The study also widens work beyond paid employment: a parent's unseen labor, the care of a home, service freely given, all of it serves neighbors and is seen by God. And the promise that your labor isn't in vain reaches back over the work you've already done. You aren't useless because you've stopped producing. You never were what you produced. If being without work has left you in a dark place, please tell someone; your leader can help you find a pastor or counselor.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not this just religion telling people to work hard and be content with their lot?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and religion has often done exactly that. The study tries to earn an answer by refusing the cheap version. It doesn't tell you to grin and bear meaningless toil; it takes the futility of work seriously and lets Ecclesiastes say that much labor feels like "vanity and a striving after wind" (Ecclesiastes 2:11). It doesn't bless every job; it insists that work that exploits a neighbor rather than serving him is no true vocation. And it turns its sharpest edge on the successful and the religious, on the idol of achievement and the pastor who worships his own work, not on the worker told to stay in his place. What it offers is a claim you can weigh: your work has a dignity God gave it, your worth doesn't rest on your output, and the good you do in love isn't finally lost.

timeline.event: Genesis opens with God at work for six days, forming, filling and ordering, and calling the work good. He makes a creature in his image and gives him a job, to work the garden and keep it (Genesis 2:15).
After the man and the woman eat, God curses not work itself but the ground, so thorns and thistles resist the hand and bread comes by the sweat of the face (Genesis 3:17-19).
Israel's psalms give language for both the dignity and the anxiety of work. Psalm 127, titled "of Solomon," warns that unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.
Ecclesiastes, traditionally linked with Solomon, looks at all the work of human hands "under the sun" and calls it vanity and a striving after wind: Scripture's own lament over the futility of toil.

Jesus, known in Nazareth as "the carpenter" (Mark 6:3), teaches that "the laborer deserves his wages" (Luke 10:7), redefines greatness as service, and warns against the idol of accumulation in the parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13-21).
Paul ends his chapter on the resurrection by telling believers to abound in the work of the Lord, because their labor is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).
Paul writes to the Colossians that whatever they do, they should work heartily as for the Lord, addressing ordinary workers and even slaves (Colossians 3:22-24).

Augustine writes On the Work of Monks, arguing that monks should do manual labor. A century later Benedict's Rule sets daily hours for both prayer and work, a pattern later summed up as "pray and work."

Martin Luther, in To the Christian Nobility, argues that the shoemaker, the smith and the farmer each have a work and office from God, taking the word calling out of the cloister and giving it back to ordinary stations.
John Calvin's final Institutes teaches that God has assigned each person a particular calling as a post to keep, shaping centuries of Protestant thought about work.

Dorothy L. Sayers gives her address Why Work?, arguing that the church has failed by treating faith as separate from the quality of a person's labor, and that a carpenter's religion first asks him to make good tables.
Lester DeKoster publishes Work: The Meaning of Your Life, arguing that work is how we make ourselves useful to others and so a primary way of loving the neighbor.
Os Guinness publishes The Call, distinguishing the primary calling to God himself from the secondary callings to particular work and stations.
N. T. Wright publishes Surprised by Hope, recovering for a wide audience the biblical hope of bodily resurrection and a renewed creation rather than a disembodied heaven.
Tim Keller, with Katherine Leary Alsdorf, publishes Every Good Endeavor, a theology of work as creation gift, toil frustrated by the fall, and service redeemed by the gospel.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for bringing your real working life into this room. Most of us keep our jobs and our faith in separate compartments, and we're about to put them back together. Three things before we start. First, you can say what's true here. You can say you hate your job, or that you've made your work your whole identity, or that you feel useless now that you've stopped working. Nobody's going to fix you or hand you career advice. Second, this study takes all work seriously as a matter of faith, the dull job and the dream job, the paid work and the unpaid, and it will never tell you your ordinary labor is beneath God's notice. Third, the teaching puts its own writer inside all of this, and I'm inside it too. Pastors can make an idol of work and hide behind busyness, and so can I. We aren't outside the problem looking in. We're workers, like you, bringing our Mondays. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only true ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the week we're about to walk into, the Monday morning and the long afternoon and the work waiting for us, because that's where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't all resolved, because work this side of the new creation is still mixed with thorns, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. Take what we said tonight back to your work this week. Try the practice, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. If tonight named something in you, that you've despised your work, or worshiped it, or never once believed God cared about it, don't carry that alone. And if work, or the loss of it, has put you somewhere darker than a hard week, stay behind or find me this week. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, agree that this is a room where people can say what's true, and name the two lies the study refuses: that ordinary work doesn't matter, and that work is everything. Walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, Before the Thorns, full discussion and practice, with extended time on work as part of the good creation and the image of a working God.
Week 3: Session 2, Thorns and Sweat, the curse on work and the honest lament of Ecclesiastes, with time to let people name the grind without shame.
Week 4: Session 3, The Lie That Splits the World, part one: the sacred-secular divide and Luther's recovery of vocation.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, Dorothy Sayers and the good table, and the turn onto the pastor and the ranking of jobs, plus practice.
Week 6: Session 4, When Work Becomes a God, the idol of identity and the Sabbath as the assault on it.
Week 7: Session 5, Our Labor Is Not in Vain, the new creation and work as love of neighbor, with care to hold it together with session 4.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the Scripture index, and what each person is carrying back to Monday, holding together the gift, the curse, the lie, the idol and the hope.

bibliography.title: Every Good Endeavor: Connecting Your Work to God's Work
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller with Katherine Leary Alsdorf
bibliography.note: The fullest modern theology of work (2012), holding together work as creation gift, toil frustrated by the fall, and service redeemed by the gospel. Background for the whole study, especially sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: Why Work, in Creed or Chaos
bibliography.author: Dorothy L. Sayers
bibliography.note: Sayers's 1942 address arguing that faith must reach the actual quality of a person's labor, and that the first thing a carpenter's religion asks of him is good tables. The sharp edge of session 3.

bibliography.title: Work: The Meaning of Your Life, a Christian Perspective
bibliography.author: Lester DeKoster
bibliography.note: A short, dense argument (1982) that work is how we make ourselves useful to others and so a primary way of loving the neighbor. Background for sessions 1, 3 and 5; the study paraphrases it in its own words.

bibliography.title: The Call: Finding and Fulfilling the Central Purpose of Your Life
bibliography.author: Os Guinness
bibliography.note: Distinguishes the primary calling to God himself from the secondary callings to our work and stations, warning against both idolizing work and dismissing it (1998). Supports sessions 3 and 4.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope: Rethinking Heaven, the Resurrection, and the Mission of the Church
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Recovers the biblical hope of bodily resurrection and a renewed creation rather than a disembodied heaven (2008). The backbone of session 5.

bibliography.title: Counterfeit Gods: The Empty Promises of Money, Sex, and Power
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: On how good gifts, including work and success, become idols that can't bear the weight we place on them (2009). Background for session 4.

bibliography.title: God at Work: Your Christian Vocation in All of Life
bibliography.author: Gene Edward Veith
bibliography.note: A clear introduction to Luther's doctrine of vocation, that God works through ordinary callings to provide for the world (2002). Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: Garden City: Work, Rest, and the Art of Being Human
bibliography.author: John Mark Comer
bibliography.note: On work and rest as built into creation from Eden onward, accessible and pastoral (2015). Further reading for sessions 1 and 4; the study doesn't draw on it directly.

bibliography.title: The Imitation of Christ
bibliography.author: Thomas a Kempis
bibliography.note: The contemplative classic counseling the troubled soul not to lean on its own striving and management, a steadying voice against the anxiety of production. Background for session 4.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Augustine's account of his restless heart, which finds rest only in God (Confessions 1.1). Background for session 4 on rest and the restlessness that drives much overwork.

bibliography.title: Visions of Vocation: Common Grace for the Common Good
bibliography.author: Steven Garber
bibliography.note: On vocation as responsibility for the world we know and love, connecting work to the love of neighbor and the common good (2014). A further voice for sessions 3 and 5.

bibliography.title: Ordinary: Sustainable Faith in a Radical, Restless World
bibliography.author: Michael Horton
bibliography.note: A defense of ordinary, unspectacular faithfulness, including ordinary work, against the pressure to be extraordinary (2014). Further reading for session 3.

furtherReading: Every Good Endeavor, Timothy Keller, for readers who want the fullest single treatment of the theology of work that anchors this study.
Why Work?, Dorothy L. Sayers, a short essay every worker should read on why faith must reach the quality of the work itself.
Surprised by Hope, N. T. Wright, for those who want to think hard about the new creation and why it means our present labor is not in vain.
Work, Lester DeKoster, a brief and bracing argument that work is love of neighbor made useful, read alongside sessions 1 and 5.
The Call, Os Guinness, for readers who want to sort out the primary calling to God from the secondary callings to their work and stations.

glossary.definition: Human labor of every honest kind, paid or unpaid, given as a gift in the garden before the fall and part of bearing the image of a God who works. Scripture treats it as good in its design, frustrated by the curse and redeemed in Christ, and the study won't flatten it into only one of those.

Calling. The medieval church kept the word for monks, priests and nuns; Luther gave it back to every station, teaching that God calls the farmer, the magistrate and the mother as truly as the priest, and serves the world through them.

The first charge to humanity in Genesis 1:28, to be fruitful, fill the earth, subdue it and have dominion, given as a blessing. It establishes work as the cultivation and care of creation, not a consequence of sin.

What the fall did to work. The curse falls on the ground rather than the worker (Genesis 3:17-19), so thorns and thistles resist the hand and bread comes by sweat. It explains why work fights back without erasing the gift it corrupted.

The lie that some work, chiefly ministry, is holy and counts to God, while ordinary work is secular and second-class. The study takes it apart: there's no caste of jobs, only work done with God or without him.
The teaching, drawn from 1 Peter 2:9, that every Christian, not a clerical class, offers his whole life as priestly service, so no honest vocation is spiritually beneath the work of ministry.

Work asked to be God, to give the worth and identity only God can give, so the job becomes the place we go to justify our existence. It's the worship of a good gift, and the gift can't bear the weight.

The commanded weekly stop from labor, given first to former slaves as liberation (Deuteronomy 5:15). It declares with body and calendar that the world runs without us, because we're creatures and not the Creator.
The deeper rest the Sabbath points toward, taken up in Hebrews 4:9-10: ceasing not only from labor but from the striving to justify ourselves, received as a gift in Christ.

The biblical hope of a renewed heavens and earth and a bodily resurrection, not a disembodied heaven, into which the good fruit of human labor and culture is carried and kept, the ground for the promise that our work is not in vain.

God's goodness poured out on all people, believer and unbeliever alike, through the ordinary structures of work and society, so that the labor of all kinds of people serves the world God loves whether or not they know him.

An old name for a listless restlessness or sloth of soul, a refusal of the good work set before us, distinguished from honest rest, and worth naming because the cure for the idol of work is not laziness but ordered rest and ordered labor together.

The worth God stitched into work by working himself and by giving work to the image-bearer before the fall, so that the most ordinary task carries a dignity that no shoddy culture and no sacred-secular lie can finally erase.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Many of us feel that our faith is large on Sunday and shrinks to nothing by Monday, as if the forty hours we spend at work were spiritually beside the point. This five-session study takes that apart. It asks what work is: the gift God gave in the garden before anything broke, the thorns the fall drove through it, the lie that splits jobs into sacred and secular, the idol work becomes when it turns into our identity, and the promise that our labor isn't in vain. It refuses two lies at once, that ordinary work doesn't matter to God and that work is everything, and it starts with the pastor, whose own work can become an idol. Any volunteer can lead it. Bring your Monday.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on work and vocation, on faith that has to survive Monday and not just Sunday, drawing on Keller, Luther and Dorothy Sayers. Before anyone assumes it's only for people who hate their jobs, hear this. It's for everyone who works, which is everyone. It says plainly that your ordinary job is holy to God, that there's no sacred tier of work and a secular tier that doesn't count. And it warns just as plainly against making your work a god. It starts with the preacher, because I've made an idol of my own work more than once. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.

quoteCards: The first worker in the Bible is God. He worked six days and called the work good.
Work isn't the curse. It's the gift the curse fell on.
A faith that can't account for the grind won't survive Monday.
God feeds the world, but he doesn't rain bread from the sky. He feeds it through the farmer, the baker, the driver and the cashier.
Dorothy Sayers asked why the church never tells a carpenter that the first thing his religion asks of him is good tables.
Good things make the most dangerous gods, and work is a very good thing.
If you can't stop, somewhere down deep you believe it all falls apart without you.
Paul ends the great resurrection chapter with a word about work. Your labor is not in vain.
